title: Simple bases and simple-reflection orbits from rational reflection data
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbf Q$ [def-weil-field], [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. Let $S\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and span $V$. For each $r\in S$ let $c_r:V\to\mathbf Q$ be linear, with $c_r(r)=2$, $c_r(S)\subseteq\mathbf Z$, and $s_r(x)=x-c_r(x)r$ permuting $S$. Assume $S\cap\mathbf Qr=\{r,-r\}$ for every $r\in S$. Then there is a subset $D\subseteq S$ that is a rational basis of $V$ such that every $r\in S$ has integer $D$-coordinates which are either all nonnegative or all nonpositive. Moreover each $r\in S$ is $s_{d_1}\cdots s_{d_k}(d)$ for some $k\geq0$ and $d,d_1,\ldots,d_k\in D$, where the rightmost reflection acts first. If $V=0$, then $S=D=\varnothing$, and the last assertion is vacuous.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.22, printed pp.610--612, especially C.21--C.22: bases exist and W times the base equals the root set; C.11 gives simple-reflection generation. The unbundled rational formulation also uses reflection uniqueness C.3.

proof.text: If $V=0$, its only vector is zero, so $S=\varnothing$; take $D=\varnothing$. Assume henceforth $V\ne0$. Each $s_r$ is a rational linear involution: $c_r(s_r x)=-c_r(x)$, hence $s_r^2x=x$. Let $W$ be the subgroup of rational linear automorphisms generated by the $s_r$. Every element permutes $S$. Two such elements agreeing on $S$ agree on every rational linear combination of $S$, hence on $V$. Thus restriction injects $W$ into the finite permutation group of $S$, and $W$ is finite.

source.place: C.1 and C.15, printed pp.607 and 611: involutions and the faithful finite permutation action

proof.text:
Choose a rational basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ and put $B_0(x,y)=\sum_i x_i y_i$ in its coordinates. Define the rational symmetric bilinear form $B(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}B_0(wx,wy)$. All summands $B_0(wx,wx)$ are nonnegative, and the identity summand is positive for $x\ne0$, so $B(x,x)>0$. For $g\in W$, the substitution $u=wg$ bijects the finite indexing set, giving $B(gx,gy)=B(x,y)$. In particular, using $s_r r=-r$ gives
$$B(x,r)=B(s_r x,s_r r)=-B(x,r)+c_r(x)B(r,r),$$
so $c_r(x)=2B(x,r)/B(r,r)$. All denominators here are positive rational numbers.

source.place: C.19--C.20, printed p.611: explicit finite-sum invariant form and reflection formula

proof.text: The family $r\mapsto c_r$ is injective. Indeed, if $c_a=c_b=f$, the formula just obtained yields $B(x,u)=0$ for all $x$, where $u=a/B(a,a)-b/B(b,b)$. Taking $x=u$ and using positivity gives $u=0$. Applying $f$ to this equality, with $f(a)=f(b)=2$, yields $B(a,a)=B(b,b)$ and hence $a=b$. This proves injectivity without assuming that roots have equal lengths.

source.place: C.20, printed p.611: the coroot formula; elementary injectivity calculation

proof.text: Use the finite index set $I=S$, $M=V$, $N=V^\vee$, $a_r=r$, $b_r=c_r$, and evaluation $p(x,f)=f(x)$. Evaluation is perfect in finite dimension: for a basis $e_i$ and its coordinate functionals $e_i^*$, a functional $F$ on $V^\vee$ is evaluation at $\sum_iF(e_i^*)e_i$; this is inverse to $V\to(V^\vee)^\vee$. The other induced dual map is the identity. Step 3 supplies the coroot injection; the root injection is the subset inclusion. All other hypotheses of [lem-sfb-spanning-reflections-root-pairing] are exactly the given normalization, integrality, spanning and reflection stability. Apply it to obtain $P$ with these same roots and coroots, both spanning, and with root reflections exactly $s_r$. It is reduced: dependence of two nonzero roots means one is a rational multiple of the other, and the assumed root-line intersection forces equality up to sign.

source.place: C.12--C.20, printed pp.610--611; Mathlib Basic.lean:260--275 packages the root/coroot compatibility

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-reduced-rational-root-pairing-base] to $P$: the index set is finite, both families span by step 4, integral pairings are the original $c_r(S)\subseteq\mathbf Z$, and reducedness was checked there. Choose its support $J$ and put $D=\{a_j:j\in J\}\subseteq S$. The roots on $J$ are linearly independent and every root or its negative is a nonnegative integer sum of them. Since $S$ spans $V$, these same roots span $V$, so $D$ is a rational basis. The displayed nonnegative sums (or their negatives) are therefore its unique coordinates, proving the required integral sign assertion.

source.place: C.21--C.22, printed p.612: base existence and its coordinate interpretation

proof.text: Let $Q(i)$ mean that $a_i=w(d)$ for a finite word $w$ in reflections $s_j$ with $j\in J$ and some $d\in D$. The empty word gives $Q(j)$ for $j\in J$. Prepending $s_j$ preserves $Q$ whenever $j\in J$. Finally, if $a_i=w(d)$, linearity and $s_d(d)=-d$ give $-a_i=w(s_d(d))$, again a word of the required kind. Thus $Q(i)$ implies $Q(\sigma_i(i))$, since $a_{\sigma_i(i)}=-a_i$. These are exactly the three hypotheses of [lem-sfb-root-base-reflection-induction]. Apply it to the same finite reduced crystallographic $P$ and its base to obtain $Q(i)$ for every $i$. Reading each word with its rightmost factor acting first gives the last assertion. No assertion that different simple roots have the same orbit is used.

source.place: C.22, printed p.612, W times the base equals the root set; Mathlib Base.lean:665--674 supplies reflection induction
